---

# Topic & Motivation

Yellowstone in June of 2018 became one of the most watched cable dramas in American television history. A significant portion of the program was shot in Montana's Gallatin County, giving viewers a romanticized view of what Montana living might be like. Following that, there was a significant increase in both housing values and tourists in the surrounding area. This served as a major driving force behind our inquiry: did the show contribute to the area's growth or was it just a coincidence?  

In this project, we examine what we refer to as the "Netflix Effect," which is the theory that the release of a well-known TV show or movie that was filmed in a particular area results in a statistically significant rise in local housing costs and rental rates. The process is combined of how media coverage increases a location's visibility, draws tourists and new residents, increases demand for housing and short-term rentals, and eventually drives up costs.

There is growing pressure on local authorities, housing advocates, and planners in filming locations regarding the affordability of housing. Land-use policy, short-term rental regulation, and regional economic planning are all directly impacted by determining whether media attention is a significant factor in housing pricing. 

We examine **six U.S. television series** with clearly identifiable filming counties:

| Show | Filming County | State | Premiere Year |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Yellowstone* | Gallatin County | MT |   2018 |
| *Breaking Bad* | Bernalillo County | NM | 2008 |
| *The White Lotus* (Season 1) | Maui County | HI | 2021 |
| *Stranger Things* | Fulton County | GA | 2016 |
| *Outer Banks* | Charleston County | SC | 2020 |
| *Ozark* | Camden County | MO | 2017 |

---

# Data Sources

Our analysis draws on four distinct data sources, each contributing a different part of the housing and media landscape.

**IMDb Public Datasets** ([datasets.imdbws.com](https://datasets.imdbws.com/)) provide structured metadata on TV titles including premiere year and show identifiers. We use this to anchor the "treatment shock", the release date for each show in our sample.

**Wikipedia** ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org)) show pages were scraped using the `rvest` package to get infobox data confirming filming locations and release years. This provides the geographic treatment assignment that IMDb alone cannot supply.

**FHFA House Price Index** ([fhfa.gov/data/hpi/datasets](https://www.fhfa.gov/data/hpi/datasets)) provides annual county-level housing price indices from 1975 to 2024. We use the 2000-base index (HPI = 100 in year 2000) as our primary housing outcome, ensuring consistent cross-county comparisons over time. The full dataset covers over 3,000 U.S. counties.

**Zillow Research — ZORI** ([zillow.com/research/data](https://www.zillow.com/research/data/)) provides monthly county-level Observed Rent Index data covering 2015–2026 for 1,287 counties. This serves as our rental market outcome variable.

**Inside Airbnb — Bozeman, MT** ([insideairbnb.com](http://insideairbnb.com/)) provides a listing-level dataset of 600 active Airbnb properties in Bozeman, including nightly price, room type, estimated occupancy, and first review date. This is used as a supplementary lens on the short-term rental market in the primary Yellowstone treatment county.

---

# Data Processing
To assemble all of these sources into one analysis panel we had to do a variety of cleaning and merging steps. 

**1. HPI: 2000-base index selected as primary outcome.**
The FHFA provides three HPI variants: a raw base, a 1990-base, and a 2000-base. We chose the 2000-base because it sets every county to an index value of 100 in year 2000, making percentage changes directly comparable across counties with very different absolute price levels. The 1990-base has a lot more missing values (38,560 vs. 8,732 for the 2000-base), and the raw index is not meaningfully comparable cross-county.

**2. ZORI: Pivoted from wide to long; annual means computed.**
Zillow provided rental data in wide format with one column per month (142 columns total). We pivoted this to long format (one row per county-month) and computed annual averages for merging with the annual HPI panel. County-years with fewer than six months of valid ZORI observations were marked as unreliable and excluded from analysis, to prevent averages based on sparse data from distorting the results.

**3. Geographic scope: Six U.S. counties only.**
Several shows in our original list, including Game of Thrones (Croatia) and The White Lotus Seasons 2 and 3 (Sicily, Thailand), were filmed internationally and have no corresponding U.S. county housing data. These were excluded. Ozark was mapped to Camden County, MO, the county containing the Lake of the Ozarks where filming primarily occurred.

**4. Airbnb: Price cleaned, extreme outliers removed.**
Nightly prices are stored as character strings (e.g., `"$90.00"`). We stripped the dollar sign and converted to numeric. Fifty-three listings (~9%) had missing prices and were dropped, as these appear to correspond to inactive listings. Listings priced above $2,000 per night were also removed as outliers so that density plots and medians reflect the typical rental market.

**5. Sample period: 2000–2024 for HPI; 2015–2025 for ZORI.**
The HPI analysis begins in 2000 to match the 2000-base normalization and to focus on the modern media era. The ZORI analysis is constrained by Zillow data availability, which begins in 2015 at the county level.

---

# Visualizations

The six figures below build progressively from broad descriptive context toward a tighter pre/post treatment comparison that will anchor the causal analysis in Stage 3.

---

## Figure 1 — HPI Trends in Treated Counties, 2000–2024

```{r fig1, fig.cap="House Price Index for each treated county, 2000–2024. Index = 100 in year 2000. Dashed vertical lines mark each show's premiere year.", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("Output/fig1_hpi_treated_trends.png")
```

**Purpose:** This figure establishes the long-run housing price trajectory for each of the six treatment counties before any causal claims are made. This graph shows us descriptive details such as where the counties were in 2000, how fast were they growing before their shows premiered, and are there any pre-existing trends that might confound a treatment effect? 

**Design choices:** We used a consistent color palette for all six figures so that each show/county is distinguishable to the viewer. The 2000-base HPI normalizes all of the counties to the same starting value; the base allows for a direct visual comparison of growth rates rather than absolute levels, without this counties with higher abolsute home values would dominate. The dashed verticle lines mark each show's premiere year, making the 'before and after' boundary immediately apparent. A line-and-point geometry is used rather than a smooth curve because the data are annual discrete observations, not continous. 

---

## Figure 2 — Event Study: HPI Relative to Premiere Year

```{r fig2, fig.cap="Each county's HPI re-indexed to 100 in its own premiere year. X-axis shows years before and after premiere (0 = premiere year).", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("Output/fig2_event_study_hpi.png")
```

In Figure 1 each county's trajectory is shown based on the shows release year but these years are different based on the show making the trajectories hard to align visually. In this figure we re-center the x-axis to zero (the premiere year) and re-index each county's HPI to 100 in that same year. This allows a direct comparison for pre and post-premiere trajectories across all six counties on a common scale. This is a typical event study design used to assess whether outcomes change after a treatment. 

**Purpose:** Each county's trajectory is displayed in Figure 1 according to the year of the program's release, however these years vary depending on the program, making it difficult to visually align the trajectories. We re-index each county's HPI to 100 in that year and re-center the x-axis to zero (the premiere year) in this graphic. This makes it possible to directly compare pre-premiere and post-premiere trends on a similar scale for each of the six counties. To determine whether results change following a therapy, this is a common event research design. 

**Design choices:** An easy-to-understand and visual comparison is produced by the shared y-axis (indexed HPI) and shared x-axis (years since debut, −8 to +6). The viewer may quickly compare pre- and post-trend slopes and determine whether or not growth appears to increase following treatment thanks to the window of time before and after. 

---

## Figure 3 — Monthly Rental Index (ZORI) in Treated Counties

```{r fig3, fig.cap="Monthly Zillow Observed Rent Index (ZORI) for each treated county. Dashed lines mark premiere year. Note limited coverage for Gallatin (MT) and Maui (HI), which only enter the Zillow dataset in late 2020.", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("Output/fig3_zori_treated_trends.png")
```

**Purpose:** While Figures 1 and 2 focus on housing purchase prices, this figure shifts to the rental market. Rental markets can react faster than purchase markets (due to transaction timelines) so the rental index may be a more sensitive and timely indicator of our 'Netflix Effect.'

**Design choices:** We use monthly rather than annual ZORI data because rental markets move quickly, looking at annual average could smooth out sharp inflection that we are trying to see. The dollar-formatted y-axis labels make the absolute rental level immediately interpretable. We include the subtitle flags on the data limitation for Gallatin and Maui as well to be transparent about data gaps in our analysis. 

---

## Figure 4 — Treated Counties vs. National Median HPI

```{r fig4, fig.cap="Treated county HPI trends overlaid with the national median HPI (thick dotted black line), 2000–2024.", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("Output/fig4_treated_vs_national_hpi.png")
```

**Purpose:** One of the challenges in this analysis was finding a way to seperate our 'Netflix Effect' from just broader macroeconomic trends. If housing prices were rising nationally then the treated counties would show increases in HPI without the media effect. This figure overlays national median HPI against each treated county, proving a visual sense of whether these counties diverged from the national trend or no around their premiere date.

**Design choices:** The national median is shown as a thick dotted black line, visually distinct from the colored solid county lines, so the reader immediately identifies it as the reference series. This figure sets up the logic for later difference-in-differences by looking at whether treted counties moved differently than the broader benchmark 

---

## Figure 5 — Airbnb Prices in Bozeman: Pre vs. Post *Yellowstone*

```{r fig5, fig.cap="Distribution of Airbnb nightly prices in Bozeman, MT for listings that entered the market before vs. after the Yellowstone premiere (June 2018). Dashed lines = group medians.", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("Output/fig5_airbnb_bozeman_prices.png")
```
 
**Purpose:** We investigated whether listings that entered the market following Yellowstone's premiere were priced differently from those that came before it using Bozeman Airbnb listing prices before and after. This chart illustrates a distributional shift rather than merely a time trend, indicating if post-premiere listings were more costly, whether the distribution shifted to the right overall, and whether the median increased.

**Design choices:** A density histogram rather than a simple bar chart is used so that both the shape of the distribution and the relative frequency are visible simultaneously. Overlapping histograms with transparency allow direct comparison. Dashed median lines create a clear summary. The x-axis is capped at $800 to focus on the typical rental market range, as the small number of extreme-price luxury listings would otherwise compress the bulk of the distribution into an unreadable sliver.

---

## Figure 6 — Pre vs. Post Premiere HPI Growth Rate

```{r fig6, fig.cap="Each point represents a treated county. X-axis = average annual HPI growth in the 5 years before premiere; Y-axis = average annual HPI growth in the 5 years after. Points above the 45-degree line grew faster post-premiere.", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("Output/fig6_pre_post_growth_scatter.png")
```

**Purpose:** The main descriptive question is succinctly in one panel in this figure. Did treated counties increase more quickly following the premiere of their show compared to their own pre-premiere trend? Each county is reduced to two figures, and the average annual HPI increase for the five years prior to and five years following the premiere is plotted against one another.

**Design choices:** The main point of the image is the 45-degree reference line. The null hypothesis of no change is represented by its slope of 1, which indicates that any county on the line had the same growth rate before and after. Counties below it had slowing, and those above it had acceleration. Although a thorough causation test is still pending in Stage 3, this figure conveys the majority of treated counties fall above the line, supporting the Netflix Effect hypothesis.
